Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

[{"id": "arka-english-main-2-prompt-long-0129", "row_sha256": "2d0d04746625b59cd99480295908cf221f149cf90fb9ed5e70cf4d0455079aab", "mode": "/prompt", "language": "en", "context": {}, "identity": false, "mode_instructions": "Organize the supplied request into a clear prompt. Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "
hey, can you help me shape a prompt for one independent fictional episode about an apartment intercom repair? i want it to read like a grounded, connected account, not a general guide to intercoms and not a finished repair report. the apartment is 4B in a six-unit building on Alder Street. Amaya lives in 4B; Bram is the building manager. Please make the recipient instruction explicit: “Amaya, not Bram.” The message about arranging access should be addressed to Amaya, not Bram, even though Bram is involved in coordinating the repair. Keep those roles clear instead of letting the manager become the person being asked to let the technician in.

The problem is with the building’s shared entry intercom. When a visitor presses 4B downstairs, Amaya’s apartment handset sometimes rings once and then goes quiet before she can answer. Other times it rings, but the person at the entrance says they can hear a low buzz and not her voice. Don’t make it fail in a perfectly consistent way; the occasional normal call is part of why the residents are trying to describe what happens. Amaya reported it on Tuesday evening after a grocery delivery waited outside. She was home, heard the first ring, and got to the handset after the sound stopped. The delivery person called her mobile, so the groceries were brought upstairs, but don’t turn that into a dramatic incident or claim the intercom caused a loss. She is not sure whether the same thing happened the previous weekend, because she had been away for part of it.

Bram has already spoken briefly with Amaya in the hallway and asked her to send a written description of the fault and a few possible times for access. He has not diagnosed the problem, promised a repair, or confirmed a visit. He says he can contact the building’s repair contractor once he has her availability. Include that distinction. The next step in the episode is for Amaya to write back with her observations and possible access windows, while Bram arranges the contractor’s visit after receiving them. Don’t have the contractor arrive, repair anything, or report a cause in this episode. The point is the coordination and the uncertainty about the fault, not a successful resolution.

For the repair details, the entrance panel has six apartment buttons and a small speaker grille. Amaya can describe what she heard from inside 4B but cannot see or test the panel while someone is downstairs. She has tried lifting the handset back onto its cradle and waiting a minute before answering another call; that seemed to help once, but she doesn’t know whether it was related. She has not opened the handset, changed its wiring, or asked another resident to take it apart. Bram has heard the low buzz once during a call from the lobby, but he was using his own mobile to speak with her and was not testing the intercom from inside her apartment. Keep these as separate observations, not proof of a particular broken component.

The building has a front door that locks automatically, and visitors normally use the intercom to reach residents. The side entrance is not an alternative for deliveries; it is kept locked and residents use it with a key. Amaya works from home on Wednesday and Friday this week, but has video meetings until noon on Wednesday. On Thursday she will be out between 1 and 4 p.m. and could not meet a technician then. She can leave work early on Monday if the contractor gives her enough notice, though she would rather offer Wednesday after noon or Friday morning first. Treat those as options she is giving, not confirmed appointments. Don’t invent exact dates, a repair window, a building policy about payment, or a deadline Bram gave her.

I’d like the final prompt to ask for a short but developed episode in connected substantive paragraphs, with a natural, ordinary quote from either Amaya or Bram included in the account. A quote like Bram saying, “Send me the times that work for you, and I’ll contact the contractor,” would fit, but make sure it doesn’t imply that the contractor has already been booked. It could include a numbered section if there’s a useful reason, for example a brief list of Amaya’s available access windows; don’t add numbering just to decorate it. The account should be easy to follow as the request moves from the reported fault to the observations and then to the access coordination. Keep the language plain and specific, with enough concrete detail to make this a distinct episode rather than a generic complaint about a noisy intercom.

Please make the last paragraph carry distinct information rather than repeating the fault or summarizing the whole account. It can note that Amaya is willing to leave the handset untouched until someone can check it, while she continues using her mobile if a visitor cannot reach her through the panel. That is her practical plan, not evidence that the intercom is fixed. Keep the account within the facts above, and don’t add a diagnosis, a completed visit, a repair result, or a final approval from either person.", "output": "Write one independent fictional episode about an apartment intercom repair. Set it in 4B of a six-unit building on Alder Street. Amaya lives in 4B, and Bram is the building manager. Make the recipient instruction explicit: “Amaya, not Bram.” Address the message arranging access to Amaya, not Bram, while keeping Bram’s role in coordinating the repair clear.

The building’s shared entry intercom is unreliable. When a visitor presses 4B downstairs, Amaya’s handset sometimes rings once and goes quiet before she can answer. At other times it rings, but the visitor reports hearing a low buzz instead of Amaya’s voice. Occasionally a call works normally. Amaya reported the problem on Tuesday evening after a grocery delivery waited outside. She was home, heard the first ring, and reached the handset after it stopped. The delivery person called her mobile, and the groceries were brought upstairs. Do not portray this as a dramatic incident or claim that the intercom caused a loss. Amaya is unsure whether the same thing happened the previous weekend because she was away for part of it.

Bram has spoken briefly with Amaya in the hallway and asked her to send a written description of the fault and possible access times. He has not diagnosed the problem, promised a repair, or confirmed a visit. He can contact the building’s repair contractor after receiving her availability. The episode should follow Amaya as she writes back with her observations and possible access windows, after which Bram can arrange the contractor’s visit. Do not have the contractor arrive, repair anything, or report a cause. Focus on coordination and uncertainty, not a resolution.

Include these separate observations without presenting them as proof of a particular fault:
1. The entrance panel has six apartment buttons and a small speaker grille. Amaya can describe what she hears inside 4B, but cannot see or test the panel while someone is downstairs.
2. She has tried putting the handset back on its cradle and waiting a minute before answering another call. That seemed to help once, though she does not know whether the two things were related. She has not opened the handset, changed its wiring, or asked another resident to take it apart.
3. Bram heard a low buzz once during a call from the lobby, but he was speaking to Amaya on his own mobile and was not testing the intercom from inside her apartment.

The front door locks automatically, and visitors normally use the intercom to reach residents. The side entrance stays locked and is used by residents with a key; it is not an alternative for deliveries. Amaya works from home on Wednesday and Friday this week, but has video meetings until noon on Wednesday. On Thursday she will be out from 1 to 4 p.m. and cannot meet a technician then. She could leave work early on Monday if the contractor gives enough notice, but she would prefer to offer Wednesday after noon or Friday morning first. Present these as options, not confirmed appointments. Do not invent exact dates, a repair window, a payment policy, or a deadline from Bram.

Write the account in connected, substantive paragraphs, with a natural, ordinary quote from Amaya or Bram. Bram might say, “Send me the times that work for you, and I’ll contact the contractor,” but the quote must not imply that the contractor has already been booked. Include a numbered section only if useful, such as a brief list of Amaya’s possible access windows. Keep the episode easy to follow as it moves from the reported fault to the observations and then to access coordination. Use plain, specific language and enough concrete detail to make it distinct from a generic complaint about a noisy intercom.

In the final paragraph, add distinct information rather than repeating the fault or summarizing the account: Amaya is willing to leave the handset untouched until someone can check it, and will continue using her mobile if a visitor cannot reach her through the panel. This is her practical plan, not evidence that the intercom is fixed. Stay within the facts above; do not add a diagnosis, completed visit, repair result, or final approval from either person."}]
